subject: jukebox
reasoning:
I'm planning out a stylized low-poly jukebox prop built from primitives, and considering whether to add a simple root joint since props may not need a full skeleton.

I'll model it after the classic Wurlitzer 1015: rounded arch top with a glowing dome, side pillars with translucent color panels, a record window, chrome grille, coin slot and button panel, speaker grille, and a base, sized roughly 1.5m tall by 0.95m wide by 0.65m deep, facing +Z and centered at x=0. Since emissive materials aren't supported, I'll fake the glow using bright flat colors, and I'm now working out the exact geometry plan using parts, extrusions, lathes, and sweeps while keeping the API usage safe and reliable.

For the structure, I'm setting up a root joint plus additional joints for a spinning turntable and tonearm to give it a nice animated touch, skipping unnecessary roles since they're optional. I'm designing the main cabinet as an extruded front-view silhouette with the classic arched top, using the outline's x-axis along world X and extruding depth along Z to build the symmetrical body shape.

Now I'm picking the color palette for a stylized 1950s jukebox look—leaning toward deep walnut wood for the body with a grain texture, paired with chrome, cream, red, teal, and amber accents, while being mindful to limit painted areas like the cabinet to keep texture density reasonable.

I'm settling on dark cherry wood body with chrome trim, glowing colored plastic pillars (amber, orange, green, red), a cream arch top with color tube lighting, and a gold grille cloth with chrome strips up front. I'm working out the dimensions—roughly 0.98m wide, 1.55m tall, 0.66m deep—and sketching the front silhouette with a base, shoulders, and a semicircular dome arch at the top characteristic of the Wurlitzer 1015 design.

Defining dome outline points...

Now thinking about the overall cabinet structure—a boxy main shell in dark wood with the front face as the extrude's front surface, onto which I'll layer additional slightly-proud extrudes for the front panel details.

For a chrome arch trim, I'm sweeping a thin tube along an arc path rather than extruding a ring shape, computing the arc's center, start point, and rotation axis using the right-hand rule to make sure it curves the correct direction.

Rather than trust the arc function's exact signature, I'll build my own helper that samples points along the arc and feed those into a sweep as a polyline path, since smooth skinning will round out the small segment angles fine with enough points. I'm also second-guessing which joint the sweep will bind to by default since bone assignment follows the nearest joint to the path's start, and adding extra joints like the turntable or tonearm could accidentally hijack that binding.

To stay safe, I'll always explicitly pass a `bone` option on static parts rather than rely on defaults, and write a small wrapper function that defaults to the base bone unless overridden. I'm also confirming how `at` and `bone` interact for placement — geometry built in model space with explicit `at` coordinates gets positioned there while still bound to the given bone — and deciding I do want a few joints (turntable, tonearm) for animation interest even though this is just a prop.

Now I'm thinking through how to make the jukebox's record mechanism visually readable: a real Wurlitzer hides records in a carousel, but a stylized front view works better with either a flat turntable and tonearm visible in the window, or a vertical magazine of edge-on records like a Seeburg. I'm leaning toward a simplified dark window recess showing a front-facing record on a tilted turntable as the clearest, most legible option.

I'll simplify to a stylized front-facing record: black disc with red label and visible groove rings, partially overlapped by others behind it to suggest depth without a full carousel.

Actually, simpler is better: just a main record, tonearm, and chrome spindle in front of a glowing amber backdrop panel, so the black record silhouette pops against the warm light.

Now I'm working out the front-view layout bottom-up — a chrome-trimmed plinth with feet at the base, then a lower grille section with cream-gold speaker cloth above it.

For the grille itself, I'm planning a recessed dark backing panel with a cloth-textured gold paint, overlaid with a row of around 11 rounded vertical chrome rods, plus a centered logo decal for brand text.

I'll use text on a title banner and maybe for selection panel numbers. For the selector buttons themselves, I'll build them from simple geometry like cylinders with color coding, placing labels on a plate beneath using text sparingly.

I'm picturing the control strip around y 0.50-0.70: a chrome-edged cream panel with two rows of ten small button cylinders in alternating red and cream, numbers drawn via a flat plane, a coin slot with chrome bezel and coin return on the right, a volume knob on the left, and a "SELECT" label. Then I'm thinking about the arch region above that holding the glowing tube-lit panel and record window.

Mapping the vertical structure: plinth at bottom, speaker grille, the control strip, then the window zone with an arched dome shape made from a rectangle topped by a semicircle, sized so the arch trim ring fits above it with colored light tubes between window and outer arch. I'm placing translucent color-changing bubble tube pillars flanking the window on each side.

Writing pillar and arch sweep code...

I should add side details since the model rotates—chrome edge posts at the corners, ribbed wood panels, and a few horizontal chrome strips with ridged lines on the flanks. The back can stay simple: a plain panel with a vent grille and power cord.

For the overall shape, I'm thinking the top dome should be a half-cylinder extruded along depth, matching the real jukebox's arched front and straight-sided profile, with a slight bevel on the extrusion edges for softness. For materials, I'm debating between classic walnut wood versus a bolder painted look—maybe deep teal with cream, chrome, and amber accents—since color choice really affects how authentic this feels.

I'll go with warm mahogany wood paired with a golden-amber glowing window and rainbow arch, adding cream/ivory trim, chrome, and black rubber for contrast. I'm settling on a specific palette: two wood tones, a stylized flat chrome, cream, amber, orange, red, green, teal, blue, yellow, black, gold, and dark red.

Now I'm working out the cabinet's dimensions and extrusion settings, choosing a small bevel for a low-poly chamfered edge that fits the stylized theme.

I'm also checking texel density for painting the cabinet surfaces — total area roughly 4m², which gives about 2.3mm per texel at this resolution, plenty sharp for the detailing.

For the wood finish I'm applying a grain texture with a small axis-aligned size for a believable wood look, and considering adding thin raised inlay strips or a framed panel detail on the sides so the flat wood doesn't look too plain.

Now I'm planning the side detailing: a few horizontal chrome accent strips arranged like streamline bands across the cabinet side, plus a cream inlay frame above them, then shifting focus to front component layout with a cream arch band positioned over the dome face.

I'm reconsidering the composition — rather than a full cream face plate covering everything, I'll keep the dark glossy wood front and add distinct elements: a chrome arched ring tracing the window outline, with an amber glowing window pane set slightly recessed behind it.

For the window's interior, I'm imagining a glowing amber-to-orange gradient backdrop, plus a custom sunburst paint function that alternates shades radiating from the center based on angle from the midpoint.

Now thinking about the record and tonearm placement in front of the cabinet window — rather than truly recessing the glass, I'll push the window plate slightly proud of the cabinet face and position the record just in front of it, so it reads as sitting behind glass without actually poking outside the cabinet profile.

I'll instead make the bezel a tube ring with radius 0.03 centered at z=0.34, so it protrudes to 0.37 in front and recedes to 0.31, letting the record sit 2cm behind the front rim. For the record itself, I'm sizing it at roughly 0.19 radius centered around (0, 0.98), positioned within the arched window frame spanning y 0.72 to 1.02.

Now I'm building the record as a stack of simple geometric pieces rather than one complex lathe shape: a black vinyl disc (thin cylinder), with plans for groove-shaded rings, a red center label, and a small chrome spindle cylinder layered on top.

Rather than using lathe geometry, I'll stick with simple cylinders for the record parts since they're lower-poly, and consider adding groove detail through a paint texture on the disc surface instead.

I realize the paint also gets applied to the side and back of the record since it depends on position, giving a subtly striped rim—acceptable but worth noting. I'll keep the groove paint for the disc and use separate flat parts for the label, since parts are painted based on where they're built in their final pose, which works fine here. Next I need to set up the tonearm as a pivoting joint anchored near the upper-right of the window.

I'm positioning the tonearm's pivot base near the left side, building a rod from pivot to tip with a chrome headshell box, plus a small counterweight cylinder behind the pivot. I'm also second-guessing whether a tonearm makes sense on a vertically mounted record given gravity, but deciding it's fine as a stylized jukebox pickup arm resting in-plane.

I'll skip the backing record magazine idea and instead consider adding a small leaning stack of records on the window's bottom ledge for visual interest.

Now I'm working out the arch geometry: a chrome trim arc around the window, then a colored tube ring inside it, making sure to align the dome and window arc centers so the curves nest properly.

Adding the outer chrome ring and leaving a 1cm wood margin at the cabinet edge, then tracing how the color tube continues vertically as pillars from the arch down past y=1.06 on both sides.

I'm calculating the total path length of this tube (about 1.945 units) and planning how to divide it into colored bands separated by chrome collars, thinking through a classic rainbow sequence along the path.

Placing the chrome separator rings using position and tangent direction from the path at evenly-spaced parameter values, sizing them as thin wide cylinders to look like clamp rings between color segments.

I'll keep the tube sides at a default smooth count rather than going faceted, since 8 sides gives enough roundness. For the glow effect I want bright, saturated colors, and I'm considering adding a dark frame layer behind the tubes to make them pop visually, though extrude outlines can't easily have holes for that.

Planning the layering: a dark channel plate extruded behind the arch region at a slightly offset z-depth, then an amber window backdrop above that, with the tubes drawn on top—each layer separated by at least a couple millimeters in z to avoid z-fighting.

Adjusting the chrome bezel and record disc depths so they sit flush against the tube front, tweaking radius and z-center values until the bezel protrudes slightly beyond the record for a realistic layered look.

For the side pillars, I'm confirming the channel plate and vertical tube segments fill the space beside the window. For the dome top, I'm adding a chrome crown arc hugging the cabinet's front arch edge to finish the top detail.

I'm also considering a small finial crest at the very top, but there's not enough room near the colored tube trim for a brand banner there, so I'm thinking about reducing the window arch radius to free up space for a marquee plate above the window instead.

Actually, I decide to skip curved arch text entirely since it would need custom curved typography — instead I'll place the "MELODY KING" brand plaque as a cream oval or shield lower down, either above the speaker grille or integrated into the control strip area.

For the control strip itself, rather than fiddling with slant rotations, I'll just build it as a flat vertical cream panel protruding slightly forward with a chrome border, housing a left bank of buttons, a centered brand plaque, and a right bank of buttons plus coin slot.
